extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetics; poets composing tragedy, comedy, or epic
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for composing and judging dramatic (tragedy/comedy) and epic poetry, focusing on plot unity, meter, diction, figurative language, and the emotional effects of devices like recognition and reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (Fabula una)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabula autem est UNA ... Una imitio unius rei est: the plot (fabula) must be one, not many — the poem should imitate one whole action with parts cohering so that if any part is removed or transposed the whole is disrupted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful work imitates a single action (with beginning, middle, end). Multiple unrelated actions or episodic collections weaken the unity and are poorer artistry (e.g., many episodic poems vs. a single integrated Iliad/Odyssey action). Ensure all incidents belong by necessity or probability to the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning, Middle, and End (Parts of a Plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poema ... habet Principium, Medium, & Finem — a complete plot must have a clear beginning, middle, and end so that the whole is intelligible and satisfying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange events so the beginning leads logically to the middle and end; the audience should apprehend the whole at once when appropriate. Length must allow perception of beginning and end together (avoid excessively long constructions that obscure the unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Appropriate Length
rubrics_metrics.description: Longitudinis autem finitio ... opus enim est ut simul perſpiciatur Principium & Finis — the magnitude must be such that the beginning and end can be perceived together; greater magnitude can be beautiful if the unity remains perceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a length suited to audience attention and memory. Epic may be larger (allows episodes and greater variety); tragedy should maintain tighter limits so that the single action remains evident in one viewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Episodic, Incongruous Insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodia ... sunt deterrimae ... ornamenta aliunde advecta, alia post alia ... neque veriſimile, neque necesse — episodes imported from elsewhere that do not belong break verisimilitude and coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not paste in attractive but unrelated episodes for show. Every episode should be organically connected by cause, necessity, or probability to the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex Plot (Peripeteia and Agnitio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplem actionem ... Implexam vero, ex qua tranſitus verum in alium ſtatum cum agnitione fit, aut peripetia aut ſimul: complex plots include peripety (reversal) and recognition (agnitio) which transform the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots that effect peripeteia and agnitio produce stronger emotional effects (pity and fear) and are generally superior for tragic imitation. Design causes so reversals/recognitions arise necessarily or by probability from the plot's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal) Definition and Role
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripetia ... admirabilis ac ſubita ... mutatio eorum, quæ aguntur, in contrarium — a sudden, striking reversal of the agent's situation tied by necessity or probability to preceding events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeteia should arise from the plot's causal sequence (not from sheer chance) and be credible within the story's probabilities. It heightens tragedy when it converts success into ruin or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agnitio (Recognition) Definition and Role
rubrics_metrics.description: Agnitio ... ex ignorantia, in cognitionem mutatio — a change from ignorance to knowledge (recognition), often bringing characters from one relation to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agnition is most effective when tied to peripeteia (simultaneous recognition and reversal), intensifying pity and fear. Focus recognition on persons rather than inanimate facts when aiming for dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality and Probability (No Gratuitous Coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oportet ... ut ex antefactis aut necessatio vinculs, aut secundum veriſimile, accidat ... non ex fortuito — reversals and recognitions should occur because of prior constitution or plausible necessity/probability, not pure chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure transitions and outcomes have causal or probable antecedents. If a plot event happens without adequate causal support it will be judged artless or implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the Probable (Verisimile) Over Mere Possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Oportet eligere impoſſibilia & probabilia potius quam poſſibilia & non probabilia — prefer the improbable-but-plausible to the merely possible-but-unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose events that feel true to human experience and narrative logic even if unusual; avoid events that are technically possible but violate probability or audience expectations of plausibility. Skilled poets may render some 'absurd' things pleasing if the rest of the poem compensates (Homer example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet vs Historian: Universals vs Particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Nam poetaſis ... potius universalia, historia singularia — the poet speaks of what could or should be (universals), while the historian records what actually happened (singular facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should aim at revealing general truths or types through plausible but not necessarily factual narratives; do not confuse poetic aims with historical reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and Economy of Words (Dicto perſpicua, non humilis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictio ... præcipue elaborandum eſt otioſis in partibus, non autem in ethicis aut iis quæ Sententiis refertæ ſint. perpolita enim Dictio prorſus obſcurat Mores & Sententias — diction should be clear, not lowly; over-polished phrasing can obscure moral and sententious content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity and appropriateness over excessive ornament, especially in moral or sententious passages. Polished diction should not sacrifice meaning or ethical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity of Diction (Perſpicua vs Humilis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perſpicua igitur eſt, quæ conſtat ex propriis nominibus; at humilis eſt ... Perſpicuitati Dictionis & ad novitatem, Productiones, & Diminutiones, & Immutationes Nominum plurimum conferunt — clarity arises from use of proper (familiar) names; novelty and certain lexical productions can enhance perspicuity if used well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proper, familiar names where clarity and persuasiveness are required (esp. in tragedy); novelty of diction can be an asset when balanced with perspicuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum of Names: Tragedy vs Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: In comoedia ... jam hoc perſpicuum ſemper fuit: postquam enim fabulam fecissent, ... nomina indiſcriminatim imponunt; In tragoedia vero nominibus iis, quæ prius facta atque uſitata, adhaerent — comedies freely invent names; tragedy tends to keep customary (familiar/historic) names to enhance persuasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose names appropriate to genre: tragedy benefits from known or plausible names to aid believability, while comedy tolerates invented or whimsical names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Metaphor and Figurative Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum vero, Metaphoris uti ... hoc enim ſolum non ab alio accipere Poſſu mus, eſt etiam indicium excellentis ingenii. pulchre enim conficere Metaphoras eſt similitudi nem perſpicere — mastery of metaphor marks exceptional genius and contributes to beauty and perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metaphors skillfully and originally; good metaphors reveal likeness and clarify, while crude or misplaced metaphors can obscure or offend. The ability to craft apt metaphors is a major mark of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation / Avoiding Mediocrity and Excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediocritas autem eſt communis omnibus partibus ... qui Metaphoris, & Linguis, & aliis formis immodice utatur, idem efficiet, atque ille qui his de industria utitur ut risum moveat — moderation across devices is crucial; excess leads to mediocrity or ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ornament, dialect, and playful diction in measured amounts. Excessive rarefaction or forced novelty (to show off) undermines artistry and can make the poem ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate Lexical Forms (Dialect/Name Types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominum autem, duplicia quidem maxime conveniunt Dithyrambis: Linguæ vero, Heroicis: Metaphorz, Iambis ... in Heroicis sane apta sint omnia supradicta: in Iambis autem, quod hi præcipue imitentur Sermonem, adhibenda sunt talia Nomina qualia in Sermonibus occurrunt — different genres favor particular lexical/dialectal choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction, names, and figurative devices to the genre and meter. Heroic poetry tolerates elevated diction and broader metaphor; iambic genres should imitate spoken speech and use names common in speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter Suitability (Heroic Meter for Epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compertum fuit experientia Metrum heroicum accommodatum esse Epopœiæ ... metrum enim heroic um gravissimum et amplissimum — epic narrative fits heroic meter; other meters suit other types of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose meters aligned with genre and action: heroic meter for long narrative epics; iambic and tetrameter for movement and lighter forms. Avoid arbitrary mixing of meters which disrupts genre expectations and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of the 'Absurd' When Compensated by Excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Oportet etiam eligere impossibilia & probabilia ... quidem quanquam primum sit falsum, quoniam ud non ita fit, neceſsario ... hoc autem falsum eſt ... idcirco ſane quanquam primum ſit falſum ... Homerus, adjectis aliis bonis, splendorem affert & illud absurdum reddit jucundum — certain improbable or seemingly absurd elements may be tolerated if the poet's overall skill makes them delightful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor implausibilities can be forgiven when skill, diction, and structural excellence compensate; but do not rely on such devices without strong artistic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Violating the Capabilities of the Art (Per Se vs Per Accidens Vices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poeticæ duplex est Vitium: aliud per se, aliud per accidens. per se quidem Vitium eſt cum aggrediatur imitari id quod fit extra facultatem ſuam: per accidens ... cum haud recte imitatur — do not attempt to imitate actions beyond the art's capacities; accidental faults come from bad imitation rather than impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not portray events or skills the art cannot render convincingly; if something cannot be imitated properly, either omit it or find an artistic means to represent it convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum and Appropriateness (Decoro/Indecoro)
rubrics_metrics.description: De decoro aut indecoro dicto aut facto alicujus non ſolum animadverten dum ratione habita ipſius facti aut dicti, utrum honeſtum an turpe ſit, ſed facientis etiam & dicentis ... — consider not only whether something said/done is decent, but who says/does it and in what context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate speech and action for decorum relative to character, time, purpose, and greater good. What might be appropriate for one speaker or situation may be indecorous in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Let Diction Obscure Moral and Sententious Content
rubrics_metrics.description: perpolita enim Dictio prorſus obſcurat Mores & Sententias — excessively worked or ornate diction can obscure morals and sententiae (insights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep moral and sententious passages clear and not over-embellished; rhetorical polish should illuminate, not hide, the ethical message.
